analysis.one_liner: Caps payday loan interest at 36%, bans rollovers and criminal collection threats, and requires state licensing of lenders.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 21 cosponsors — 19 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent — but the House Financial Services Committee took no action on it, and it died without ever receiving a vote in the 108th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made payday loans unlawful in any state that did not license and strictly regulate them under standards set by the Federal Reserve. It capped interest rates at 36 percent a year for loans made by banks, capped loan amounts at $300 and fees at $5, banned rolling loans over, barred lenders from threatening borrowers with criminal charges when a check bounces, and banned forced arbitration clauses. Borrowers would have gained the right to sue lenders for damages. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Financial Services Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Payday borrowers — disproportionately low-income workers living paycheck to paycheck — would have gained the most. The bill would have ended the worst practices in the trade: loans that chain a borrower into weeks or months of repeated fees, triple-digit annual interest rates, criminal charges threatened over bounced checks, and fine-print clauses forcing borrowers into arbitration instead of court. Because the bill treated a payday loan as made where the borrower receives the money, it would also have stopped lenders from partnering with banks to sidestep state interest-rate caps. Borrowers who were harmed could have sued for real damages plus $1,000 per violation and attorney's fees.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual interest rate on bank-made payday loans at the lesser of 36 percent or the state's legal maximum, ending the triple-digit-rate bank partnerships.
Bans rolling over or re-issuing a payday loan within 30 days, the mechanism that turns a two-week loan into months of debt, and bars lenders from accepting repayment financed by another payday loan.
Caps any payday loan at $300 and any administrative fee at $5, and limits bounced-check fees to $15.

Prohibits payday lenders from bringing criminal actions or threatening criminal prosecution against borrowers whose checks bounce, and from requiring borrowers to give up their day in court through mandatory arbitration clauses.

Requires states to license payday lenders with public hearings, $50,000 surety bonds per location whose proceeds go to harmed consumers, and a private right of action letting borrowers sue for actual, consequential, and punitive damages plus $1,000 statutory damages and attorney's fees per violation.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders and the banks that financed or fronted their loans would have borne the cost. A 36 percent annual rate cap, a $5 maximum fee, a $300 loan limit, and a ban on rollovers would have made the standard two-week, high-fee payday loan unprofitable, effectively ending legal payday lending in states that did not rewrite their laws to meet the federal minimums. Borrowers who relied on these loans and had no alternative source of quick cash would also have lost access to the product.

drawbacks.text: A 36 percent annual rate, a maximum $5 fee, and a $300 principal cap would make the standard payday loan model unprofitable, so the bill would have effectively shut down most legal payday lending rather than regulated it — leaving some borrowers with no short-term credit option and pushing them toward overdrafts, unpaid bills, or illegal lenders.

Because payday loans would be unlawful in any state whose law the Federal Reserve Board determined did not meet the bill's minimum licensing and rate requirements, the bill was effectively a federal mandate on states: states that chose not to license payday lenders at all would see the product banned outright, and states would lose their own judgment over whether to permit it.

The bill regulated one side of the market only — it imposed no requirement that banks or credit unions offer affordable small-dollar alternatives, so it removed a product many borrowers used without guaranteeing anything to take its place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections were real and well targeted at the practices that trap borrowers: rollover bans, the $300 principal cap, a $5 fee cap, the ban on criminal collection threats, and a private right of action all attack the specific mechanics of the payday debt cycle. The honest drawback is that a 36 percent annual rate with a $5 fee leaves no room for the high-cost, high-default small loans the industry says it must charge for, so the bill would likely have ended legal payday lending in most states rather than tamed it. That would have been a genuine gain for borrowers who avoid the loans, and a real loss for the small share of borrowers with no other access to quick cash, unless states filled the gap. Weighing the two, the bill came down on the side of people who lose the most to these loans, but it offered no replacement credit for those the industry would claim to serve.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to its Financial Services Committee, which passed it along to a subcommittee that never took it up, and it died quietly when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the Payday Borrower Protection Act of 2003 on June 10, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
Twenty-one members joined as cosponsors — 19 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent — according to the bill's cosponsor list and the introduction roll call in the bill text.

On June 17, 2003, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and the public record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress.
The bill received no further action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and was not reintroduced action taken up in that Congress.

The bill would have overridden the prevailing industry structure by treating a payday loan as made in the borrower's state, closing the route lenders used to export high-rate loans from permissive states and through partner banks.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders came out ahead: no cap, no licensing requirement, and no rollover ban was enacted, so loans at annual rates of several hundred percent remained legal, and banks could keep lending to payday companies.

for.name: Rep. Bobby Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on June 10, 2003.

for.name: Rep. Phil English
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only Republican cosponsor.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only Independent cosponsor.

against.name: Michael Oxley
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; the committee never held a markup or voted on it, and it was sent to a subcommittee that took no action.

against.name: Payday lending industry (led by the Community Financial Services Association)
against.what_they_did: Actively lobbied Congress against federal rate caps and lending restrictions during this period, as widely reported.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic — 19 of 21 cosponsors were Democrats, joined by one Republican (Phil English) and one Independent (Bernie Sanders) — and the House never held a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill requires Federal Reserve-approved state licensing, caps rates at 36 percent, caps loans at $300 and fees at $5, and bans rollovers — terms under which the standard payday model of short, high-fee, repeatedly renewed loans cannot operate, so lending would effectively end in most states. Payday loan fees of 400 percent and more fall on low-income workers who can least afford them.

Banks would be barred from making payday loans above 36 percent or financing payday lenders that do not comply with state law, cutting off the 'rent-a-bank' structure banks used to originate payday loans at triple-digit rates across state lines. Those partnerships move fees from borrowers' pockets to bank and lender revenue.
